chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi Nasr from Muhammad ibn Sama'ah from Abd al-Hamid ibn Awadd from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who buys a beast of burden but does not have the cash for it, so he goes to one of his companions and says, 'So-and-so, pay the price of this beast for me, and the profit will be between me and you.' So he pays for him, and the beast dies. He said, 'The price is upon both of them, because if there was profit in it, it would be between them both.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a beast of burden dying when bought on credit with a partner who paid the cash?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the principle of *al-ghurm bi al-ghunm* (liability follows profit) is applied to a specific credit transaction where a partner advances the cash for a beast of burden. The Imam rules that if the beast dies, both parties bear the cost because the potential profit was shared, thereby validating the risk-sharing structure despite the initial credit arrangement. This highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on equitable risk distribution in commercial partnerships.
